extracted.intended_audience: employers, independent contractors, labor attorneys, HR professionals, and Wage and Hour Division enforcement officials
extracted.subtask_description: Federal regulation providing interpretive guidance for determining whether a worker is an employee or an independent contractor under the Fair Labor Standards Act using an economic-reality analysis. It describes the overall inquiry, enumerates multiple factors, and explains how to apply them across contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretive purpose and reliance
rubrics_metrics.description: These interpretations are intended to serve as a 'practical guide to employers and employees' as to how the Department will seek to apply the Act. The Administrator of the Wage and Hour Division will use these interpretations to guide performance of their duties unless directed otherwise by authoritative court decisions or reexamination. To the extent prior administrative rulings, interpretations, practices, or enforcement policies are inconsistent or in conflict with the interpretations stated in this part, they are rescinded. The interpretations may be relied upon in accordance with section 10 of the Portal-to-Portal Act (29 U.S.C. 259).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This establishes the rule's status as binding departmental interpretive guidance (Skidmore-style deference), signals that prior inconsistent guidance is withdrawn, and permits regulated parties to rely on these interpretations consistent with Portal-to-Portal Act protections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relevance of independent contractor or employee status under the Act
rubrics_metrics.description: The Act's minimum wage, overtime pay, and recordkeeping obligations apply only to workers who are covered employees. Workers who are independent contractors are not covered by these protections. Labeling employees as 'independent contractors' does not make these protections inapplicable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determinations hinge on substance (economic realities), not labels; ensure analysis focuses on actual working relationship rather than contractual labels or titles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economic dependence as the ultimate inquiry
rubrics_metrics.description: A determination focuses on the economic realities of the worker's relationship with the potential employer and whether the worker is either economically dependent on the potential employer for work or in business for themself. An 'employee' is an individual whom an employer suffers, permits, or otherwise employs to work; an 'independent contractor' is in business for themself. Economic dependence does not focus on the amount of income earned or whether the worker has other income sources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The central question is whether the worker is economically dependent on the employer; factual circumstances across multiple factors are used to answer this ultimate inquiry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economic reality test / totality-of-the-circumstances
rubrics_metrics.description: Multiple factors assessing the economic realities of the working relationship are used to determine economic dependence. These factors are tools or guides to conduct a totality-of-the-circumstances analysis. The outcome does not depend on isolated factors but upon the circumstances of the whole activity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No single factor or subset is necessarily dispositive; weight of each factor depends on the facts and circumstances. The six enumerated factors guide the assessment, but they are not exhaustive and additional factors may be considered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Opportunity for profit or loss depending on managerial skill
rubrics_metrics.description: Considers whether the worker has opportunities for profit or loss based on managerial skill (including initiative, business acumen, or judgment) that affect economic success or failure in performing the work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Relevant facts include whether the worker can meaningfully negotiate charges or pay, accepts/declines jobs, chooses order/time of jobs, engages in marketing or advertising, hires others, purchases materials/equipment, or rents space. If a worker has no opportunity for profit or loss, this factor suggests employee status. Note: decisions like working more hours or taking more jobs when paid a fixed rate generally do not reflect managerial skill indicative of independent-contractor status.

rubrics_metrics.name: Investments by the worker and the potential employer
rubrics_metrics.description: Considers whether investments by a worker are capital or entrepreneurial in nature. Costs of tools/equipment for a specific job, labor costs, and costs unilaterally imposed by the employer are not evidence of capital or entrepreneurial investment and indicate employee status.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Capital/entrepreneurial investments indicate independent-contractor status when they support an independent business (e.g., enabling more/ different work, reducing costs, extending market reach). Compare the types of investments (not just dollar amounts) between worker and employer on a relative basis; worker investments need not equal employer's but should be similar in kind to suggest independent operation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Degree of permanence of the work relationship
rubrics_metrics.description: Weighs in favor of employee status when the relationship is indefinite in duration, continuous, or exclusive. Weighs in favor of independent-contractor status when the relationship is definite in duration, non-exclusive, project-based, or sporadic based on the worker marketing services to multiple entities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seasonal or temporary nature alone does not necessarily indicate independent-contractor status. If lack of permanence is due to industry-specific operational characteristics, it is not necessarily indicative of independent-contractor status unless the worker is exercising independent business initiative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nature and degree of control
rubrics_metrics.description: Considers the potential employer's control, including reserved control, over performance of the work and the economic aspects of the relationship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Relevant facts include whether the employer sets schedule, supervises work performance, limits ability to work for others, uses technological means to supervise (e.g., devices/electronic monitoring), reserves right to supervise or discipline, or controls prices/rates and marketing. Actions taken solely to comply with laws/regulations are not indicative of control; actions beyond legal compliance that reflect the employer's own compliance methods, safety, quality, or customer-service standards may indicate control. More indicia of employer control favors employee status; more indicia of worker control favors independent-contractor status.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extent to which the work performed is an integral part of the potential employer's business
rubrics_metrics.description: Considers whether the work performed is critical, necessary, or central to the potential employer's principal business. This factor concerns the function performed (not whether a particular individual is integral).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the worker's function is integral to the employer's principal business, this weighs toward employee status; if not central, it weighs toward independent-contractor status.

rubrics_metrics.name: Skill and initiative
rubrics_metrics.description: Considers whether the worker uses specialized skills and whether those skills contribute to business-like initiative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lack of specialized skills or dependence on employer training indicates employee status. The mere presence of specialized skills is not itself indicative of independent-contractor status because both employees and independent contractors may be skilled; focus on whether the worker uses skills in a business-like way (initiative) that shows they are in business for themself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Additional factors
rubrics_metrics.description: Additional factors may be relevant in determining employee or independent-contractor status if they indicate whether the worker is in business for themself rather than economically dependent on the employer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The six enumerated factors are not exhaustive; consider other indicia that inform the economic-dependence inquiry on a case-by-case basis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of these criteria across agency regulations
rubrics_metrics.description: Where other parts of the CFR address specific industries (e.g., sharecroppers, tenant farmers, forestry/logging with ≤8 employees), the criteria set forth in §§ 795.100 through 795.110 are used to determine whether individuals are employees or independent contractors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This ensures consistent application of the economic-reality factors across agriculture and limited-employee forestry/ logging regulations and signals cross-part applicability of the rule's factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compliance requirements — reporting, recordkeeping, and regulatory familiarization
rubrics_metrics.description: This rule provides guidance for analyzing employee or independent-contractor status under the FLSA. It does not create any new reporting or recordkeeping requirements for businesses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department estimates regulatory familiarization time at 1 hour per firm (per-entity cost example: $52.80 using fully loaded median hourly wage of a Compensation, Benefits, and Job Analysis Specialist multiplied by 1 hour) and 0.5 hour per independent contractor (per-entity cost example: $11.73 using median hourly wage of independent contractors). These are average estimates and the Department adjusted the IRFA estimates accordingly.
